item.title: Ghostcommit AI Prompt Injection PoC and Critical Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS
item.content:encoded:
Critical Zimbra Flaw Could Let Crafted Emails Run Malicious Code in User Sessions — Must Read

Zimbra is urging customers to update to version 10.1.19 to fix a critical stored XSS flaw in the Classic Web Client that could let crafted emails run malicious code when opened. Successful exploitation could expose mailbox data, session information, or account settings.

  • Zimbra is urging customers to apply updates for a critical stored cross-site scripting flaw affecting the Classic Web Client.
  • The flaw could let specially crafted emails execute malicious scripts in a user's session when the email is opened.
  • Zimbra said exploitation could allow access to mailbox information, session data, or account settings.
  • The vulnerability has not yet been assigned a CVE identifier, and Zimbra has not mentioned any in-the-wild exploitation.
  • Users are recommended to update to Zimbra Collaboration Suite version 10.1.19 for optimal protection.

'Ghostcommit' hides prompt injection in images to fool AI agents, steal secrets — Should Read

Researchers demonstrated “Ghostcommit,” a prompt-injection technique that hides malicious instructions in an image inside a pull request, bypassing AI code reviewers that don’t inspect images. Once merged, coding agents may follow the hidden instructions and leak repository secrets by encoding them into seemingly harmless source code.

  • Researchers from the University of Missouri-Kansas City’s ASSET Research Group built a proof-of-concept attack called Ghostcommit that hides malicious instructions inside a PNG image in a pull request.
  • The attack uses an AGENTS.md file that appears to describe ordinary build hygiene but points an AI coding agent to an image containing instructions to read a repository’s .env file and encode its contents as integers in source code.
  • The researchers reported that CodeRabbit’s default configuration excludes image files from review and that Bugbot returned no findings, allowing the image-based prompt injection to pass review.
  • In one end-to-end run, Cursor driving Claude Sonnet followed the hidden instructions and emitted a 311-integer constant that decoded byte-for-byte to the entire .env file.
  • The researchers found that the coding tool affected outcomes more than the model, with Cursor and Antigravity leaking secrets under multiple models while Claude Code refused under every model tested.
